title: Retrieval: Week One
focus: No new material. Blank page, six templates per lane, then the timed redo. Retrieval is where the memory actually forms.

cards.title: Arrays and Strings: blind recall
cards.trigger: Six triggers, one page. If you cannot name the trigger you will not recall the template under pressure.
cards.recall: Paper, not keyboard. Write all six templates from Days 1 to 6 in this lane: two pointers, hashmap complement, binary search boundary, prefix sum with map, Kadane, interval merge. Then open and diff yours against these.
template: # The six openings. If any of these is not instant, that is your homework.
lo, hi = 0, len(a)                          # boundary binary search
seen = defaultdict(int); seen[0] = 1        # prefix sum count
keyInsights: Choosing the pattern is the graded step. Once chosen, the code is typing
Two pointers needs sorted. Prefix-map does not. That distinction decides half of these
If a template came out wrong, redo the original day tomorrow, not next month
cards.trap: The seductive failure today is re-reading and feeling fluent. Recognition is not recall. If your pen did not move, you learned nothing this hour.

cards.title: Structures and Design: blind recall
cards.trigger: Which container, and why not the other one.
cards.recall: From memory: bracket matcher, level-drain queue, size-k heap with the inversion, trie insert, monotonic deque with both evictions, monotonic stack. Say the complexity of each before you check.
template: # The choosing table. Recite it before you look.
# best repeatedly ............ heap; k smallest needs a MAX-heap
# max over a moving window ... monotonic deque, O(n)
keyInsights: Heap gives you the best element, not sorted order. If you need order you wanted sorting
Monotonic deque beats a heap for windows because expiry is a position test, not a value test
Trie beats a hash set only when the query is about prefixes. Otherwise it is strictly worse
cards.trap: Under time pressure people reach for a heap when a deque is linear. Cost yourself the log factor once here and you will not do it in the room.

cards.title: Trees: blind recall
cards.trigger: Down or up. Answer that first, every time.
cards.recall: From memory: postorder depth, level-drain BFS, range-bound BST validation, recursive LCA, the diameter global-versus-return split, the balance sentinel. For each, say down or up before you write it.
template: def down(node, state):        # preorder: parent hands context to child
def up(node):                 # postorder: child hands an answer to parent
# and the third shape: up(), but RECORD something the parent cannot use
keyInsights: Three shapes cover almost every tree question: push down, pull up, pull up while recording a global
Space is O(h) and degrades to O(n) on a skewed tree. Say both
BFS is only correct when the question is about levels or shortest hops. Otherwise DFS is simpler
cards.trap: The LCA base case, returning the node when it equals p or q, is the line people forget under pressure. Write it twice today.

cards.title: DP: blind recall
cards.trigger: If you cannot say what dp[i] means in one English sentence, you do not have a solution yet.
cards.recall: For each of the six, write the state definition as a sentence FIRST, then the recurrence, then the base cases. Only then the code. Do not skip straight to code, that is the habit this day exists to break.
template: # The four-line ritual. Every DP, every time, out loud.
# 3. BASE       the smallest states, stated explicitly
# 4. ORDER      the loop order that makes dependencies already computed
for c in range(cap, w - 1, -1):   # 0/1: each item once
for c in range(w, cap + 1):       # unbounded: unlimited copies
keyInsights: Wrong state definition is the root cause of almost every failed DP, not a wrong recurrence
Loop direction on the rolled knapsack is the single highest-value fact in this lane
LIS in O(n log n) is the one DP here that is not really DP. Know it as its own thing
cards.trap: Writing the code before the sentence. Under interview pressure that produces a table you cannot debug, and you will not have time to restart.

cards.title: Graphs: blind recall
cards.trigger: Unweighted means BFS. Non-negative weights means Dijkstra. Negative or hop-limited means Bellman-Ford.
cards.recall: From memory: grid flood fill, the choose-explore-unchoose skeleton, DSU find and union with both optimisations, Dijkstra with the stale skip, Bellman-Ford with the snapshot, Floyd-Warshall with k outermost.
template: # The decision tree. Recite before you look.
# negative edges, or 'at most k' ... Bellman-Ford + snapshot
# all pairs, V small ............... Floyd-Warshall, k outermost
keyInsights: Reading the weights before choosing the algorithm saves you from the most expensive mistake in this lane
DSU answers connectivity but never gives you a path. If they want the path, it is the wrong tool
Backtracking on a graph needs the visited mark removed on the way out. On a grid flood fill it usually does not
cards.trap: Reaching for Dijkstra on an unweighted graph. It works, and it is a log factor slower, and a Google interviewer will ask you why you did that.
